questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 504 B, Physics Two?
options: A Brief course: an overview of about five minutes and six lectures of about ten minutes, the second physics Foundations course in Anderson Engineering
An optional elective outside the Foundations
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format and its place in the Foundations.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour, not a substitute for a semester.
C is wrong: It is a Foundations course in Anderson Engineering.
D is wrong: Mechanics is Physics One; this course is electricity and magnetism.

questions.q: Which course does the overview call the natural mathematical companion to Physics Two?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.7: The laws of this course are written with flux and line integrals and the theorems of Gauss and Stokes.
A is wrong: That is Course Zero, not a mathematics course.
C is wrong: Physics One is a prerequisite, not the mathematical companion.
D is wrong: The overview names Calculus Two as the companion.

questions.q: Which MIT OpenCourseWare subject is the backbone of this course?
options: 8.02, Physics Two: Electricity and Magnetism, Spring 2019
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.9: The overview credits Dr Peter Dourmashkin and colleagues.
A is wrong: That is a mechanics subject.
B is wrong: That is a mathematics subject.
C is wrong: That is a circuits subject.

questions.q: About what is the elementary charge?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: Protons and electrons carry charge of this size, of opposite sign.
B is wrong: That is the Coulomb constant k in N·m²/C².
C is wrong: A coulomb is an enormous number of elementary charges.
D is wrong: That number is Planck's constant in J·s.

questions.q: Which two facts about electric charge does the lecture call fundamental?
options: Charge is conserved, and charge is quantised in multiples of the elementary charge
Charge is always positive, and it is created by friction
Charge depends on speed, and it decays over time
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.3: The total charge of an isolated system never changes, and observed charges on isolated particles are whole-number multiples of e.
B is wrong: Charge comes in two kinds, and rubbing only moves charge from one body to another.
C is wrong: Charge is conserved; it does not decay.
D is wrong: Charge moves freely in conductors, not insulators.

questions.q: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, what happens to the Coulomb force between them?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law: force is proportional to 1/r².
A is wrong: That would be an inverse law, not an inverse-square law.
C is wrong: The force decreases with distance.
D is wrong: The force depends strongly on distance.

questions.q: How does the electric repulsion between two protons compare with their gravitational attraction?
options: It is about ten times larger
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.6: Gravity dominates planetary motion only because large bodies are nearly neutral.
A is wrong: Electric forces are enormously stronger.
B is wrong: The ratio is the other way round.
D is wrong: The ratio is about 10³⁶.

questions.q: What is the principle of superposition for electric forces?
options: Forces add as numbers, ignoring direction
Charges cancel each other's fields completely
The force on a charge is the vector sum of the forces from each of the others
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.7: It is an experimental fact, and it lets every problem be built from pairs.
A is wrong: All charges contribute.
B is wrong: They add as vectors.
C is wrong: Fields add; they cancel only in special places.

questions.q: How is the electric field at a point defined?
options: As the charge at that point divided by its mass
As the total charge in the universe divided by the distance
As the work done to bring the test charge from infinity
As the force on a small positive test charge there, divided by that charge
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: Its units are newtons per coulomb, or volts per metre.
A is wrong: That does not define a field.
B is wrong: The field is defined by the force on a test charge.
C is wrong: That gives the potential energy, not the field.

questions.q: Why do electric field lines never cross?
options: Because the field has only one direction at each point
Because they repel each other like charges
Because they exist only inside conductors
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.10: If two lines crossed, the field would have two directions at the crossing point.
B is wrong: Field lines spread and bend; they are not always parallel.
C is wrong: Field lines are a drawing device, not charged objects.
D is wrong: Field lines fill space around charges.

questions.q: Two +1 microcoulomb charges are 1 m apart. What is the field at a point 1 m beyond the right-hand charge?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: The near charge gives 9,000 N/C and the far charge, 2 m away, gives one quarter of that, 2,250 N/C, both to the right.
A is wrong: The field is zero at the midpoint, not beyond the charges.
C is wrong: The far charge is twice as far, so it contributes a quarter, not the same amount.
D is wrong: Both fields point the same way and add; they do not subtract.

questions.q: What is the acceleration of a charge q of mass m in a uniform field E?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.14: It accelerates like a mass in uniform gravity, as in a cathode ray tube or inkjet printer.
B is wrong: The acceleration grows with E.
C is wrong: This inverts the ratio.
D is wrong: Force divided by mass gives acceleration.

questions.q: For a flat surface in a uniform field, what is the electric flux?
options: The field times the area, whatever the tilt
The field divided by the area
The field times the area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the surface normal
The field times the sine of the angle with the normal
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.2: Only the component of the field perpendicular to the surface contributes.
A is wrong: Tilt matters; a surface parallel to the field has zero flux.
B is wrong: Flux grows with area.
D is wrong: The factor is the cosine of the angle with the normal.

questions.q: What does Gauss's law state?
options: The flux through a closed surface is always zero
The flux depends on the shape of the surface
The field is the same everywhere on any closed surface
The electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: Charges outside contribute no net flux, because every line that enters also leaves.
A is wrong: That is Gauss's law for magnetism.
B is wrong: For a given enclosed charge, the flux is the same for any closed surface.
C is wrong: Only symmetry makes the field uniform on a well-chosen surface.

questions.q: What does Gauss's law give for the field of a point charge Q?
options: Q / ε₀, the same at all r
Q / (4π ε₀ r²), recovering Coulomb's law
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.6: A spherical surface of radius r has flux E · 4πr² = Q/ε₀.
A is wrong: That is the form for a line of charge.
B is wrong: The flux is constant; the field falls as 1/r².
C is wrong: Only inside a conductor is the field zero.

questions.q: Using Gauss's law, how does the field of a long straight line of charge depend on distance r?
options: It falls off as 1/r: E = λ/(2π ε₀ r)
It does not depend on r
It grows in proportion to r
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: A cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L encloses λL and has flux E·2πrL.
B is wrong: That is the point-charge result.
C is wrong: That is the large-sheet result.
D is wrong: That is the field inside a uniformly charged ball.

questions.q: What is the field of a large flat sheet with charge density σ?
options: σ/(2ε₀), the same at every distance
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.9: A pillbox through the sheet has flux 2EA through its ends and encloses σA.
A is wrong: That is the field between two oppositely charged plates.
B is wrong: A sheet's field does not fall off with distance.
C is wrong: Zero is the field outside a pair of opposite sheets.

questions.q: Where does excess charge sit on a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?
options: On its outer surface, because the field inside the material is zero
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: Any internal field would move the mobile charges until it vanished.
B is wrong: That would make a field inside the conductor.
C is wrong: Charges move apart to the surface.
D is wrong: Charge crowds at sharp points but is spread over the whole outer surface.

questions.q: Why does a car's metal body protect occupants from a lightning strike?
options: Rubber tyres insulate the car from the ground
A hollow conductor shields its interior, as in a Faraday cage
The field inside a conductor is at its strongest
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.12: With no charge in the cavity, the field inside a hollow conductor is zero whatever happens outside.
A is wrong: The lecture credits the conducting shell, not the tyres.
C is wrong: Metal conducts the charge around the outside; it does not repel it.
D is wrong: The field inside a conductor in equilibrium is zero.

questions.q: Why are lightning rods pointed?
options: Points reduce the field to zero
Charge crowds where a conductor's surface is sharply curved, so the field is strongest near points
Points make the rod an insulator
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.13: For the same reason, high-voltage equipment is made with smooth, rounded surfaces.
A is wrong: Points make the field stronger.
C is wrong: Shape does not change the material.
D is wrong: The reason is the field near curved surfaces.

questions.q: What is a volt?
options: A joule per coulomb, the unit of electric potential
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.2: Potential is potential energy per unit charge.
B is wrong: That is an ampere.
C is wrong: That is a unit of electric field.
D is wrong: That is a watt.

questions.q: Why is it often easier to find the potential of several charges than their field?
options: Potential does not depend on distance
Potential is a scalar, so contributions add as numbers
Potential has more components than the field
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.4: The potential of a point charge is kq/r, and the field then comes by differentiation.
A is wrong: It falls as 1/r.
C is wrong: Only special points have zero potential.
D is wrong: It has none: it is a scalar.

questions.q: How is the electric field related to the potential?
options: The field equals the potential times the distance
The field is the integral of the potential
The field is minus the gradient of the potential
The field is parallel to equipotential surfaces
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: The field points where the potential falls fastest; between plates, V = E d.
A is wrong: The potential difference equals field times distance in a uniform field, not the other way round.
B is wrong: The field is a derivative of the potential.
D is wrong: The field is perpendicular to equipotentials.

questions.q: How is the electric field related to equipotential surfaces?
options: It has no fixed relation to them
It is always perpendicular to them
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.6: Moving along an equipotential takes no work, just as a gradient is perpendicular to level sets.
A is wrong: Then moving along them would take work.
B is wrong: The field need not vanish on an equipotential.
C is wrong: The relation is fixed: perpendicular.

questions.q: What is the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor with plate area A and separation d?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: The field is σ/ε₀, the voltage is that times d, and σ = Q/A, so C = Q/V = ε₀A/d.
A is wrong: Capacitance grows with area and falls with separation.
B is wrong: This inverts the dependence on ε₀.
D is wrong: Capacitance is Q divided by V.

questions.q: Two 10 cm square plates are 1 mm apart in air. About what is the capacitance?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.10: C = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.01 / 0.001 ≈ 8.9 × 10⁻¹¹ F.
A is wrong: That is a million times too large.
B is wrong: The ratio A/d is 10 m, not 0.1 m.
D is wrong: A farad is very large; this plate pair is tiny.

questions.q: Two 6 μF capacitors are connected in series. What is the combined capacitance?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.11: In series the reciprocals add: 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3.
A is wrong: That is the parallel combination.
B is wrong: Series capacitance is less than either one.
D is wrong: Capacitances do not multiply.

questions.q: What does a dielectric do in a capacitor?
options: It increases the capacitance by a factor κ and lets it withstand higher voltage
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.12: Polarisation of the material partly cancels the field inside.
A is wrong: It increases it.
B is wrong: A dielectric is an insulator.
D is wrong: It raises both capacitance and breakdown voltage.

questions.q: What energy is stored in a capacitor C charged to voltage V?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.13: Equivalently ½QV, stored in the field with energy density ½ ε₀ E².
A is wrong: The factor one half is missing.
B is wrong: That is the charge Q, not an energy.
C is wrong: The voltage is squared.

questions.q: Why does a lamp light at once although electrons drift slowly along the wire?
options: Electrons travel at the speed of light in wires
The lamp stores charge in advance
The signal travels at nearly the speed of light because the field is set up along the wire almost at once
Current flows only at the battery
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.3: Drift speeds are often under a millimetre per second.
A is wrong: They drift slowly.
B is wrong: A lamp does not store charge.
D is wrong: Current flows throughout the circuit.

questions.q: What is the resistance of a wire of length L, area A, and resistivity ρ?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Long thin wires have more resistance than short thick ones.
A is wrong: Resistance grows with length, not area.
C is wrong: Resistance is proportional to resistivity.
D is wrong: Resistance falls as the area grows.

questions.q: About what current does a 2,000 W kettle draw from a 230 V supply?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.6: I = P/V = 2000/230 ≈ 8.7 A.
A is wrong: That inverts the ratio.
B is wrong: That multiplies instead of dividing.
C is wrong: That is far too small for a kettle of this power.

questions.q: Why are household outlets wired in parallel?
options: So each appliance sees the full supply voltage and can be switched independently
So appliances share the same current
So the total resistance is as large as possible
So one switch turns everything off
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: Parallel elements share the same voltage.
B is wrong: That is series wiring.
C is wrong: Parallel wiring lowers resistance.
D is wrong: Parallel wiring lets appliances work independently.

questions.q: What does Kirchhoff's junction rule express?
options: Conservation of energy around a loop
That all currents in a circuit are equal
Conservation of charge: current in equals current out at a junction
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.9: The loop rule, by contrast, follows from the field being conservative.
A is wrong: That is the loop rule.
B is wrong: Ohm's law is a separate material property.
C is wrong: Currents divide at junctions.

questions.q: A 12 V battery drives a 2 Ω resistor in series with two 8 Ω resistors in parallel. What current flows from the battery?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.10: The parallel pair is 4 Ω, the total is 6 Ω, and 12/6 = 2 A.
B is wrong: That is the current in each 8 Ω resistor.
C is wrong: That treats all three resistors as in series, 18 Ω.
D is wrong: That ignores the parallel pair.

questions.q: What is the time constant of a 10 kΩ resistor with a 100 μF capacitor, and how charged is the capacitor after one time constant?
options: 1 second; about 63 per cent of its final charge
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.12: τ = RC = 10⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 1 s, and 1 − e⁻¹ ≈ 0.63.
A is wrong: It takes about five time constants to be essentially full.
C is wrong: RC is 1 s, and the fraction is 63 per cent.
D is wrong: RC is 1 s; 37 per cent is what remains during discharge.

questions.q: When a capacitor charges from a battery through a resistor, what fraction of the battery's energy is stored in the capacitor?
options: Exactly one half, whatever the resistance
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.13: The other half becomes heat in the resistor; resistance sets the speed, not the split.
A is wrong: Half is lost as heat.
C is wrong: The split is independent of R.
D is wrong: That is the charge fraction after one time constant.

questions.q: What happens when a bar magnet is cut in half?
options: You get two smaller magnets, each with both poles
You get a separate north pole and south pole
Each half becomes a north pole
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.2: No isolated magnetic pole has been found; field lines form closed loops.
B is wrong: Poles have never been isolated.
C is wrong: Each half is still a magnet.
D is wrong: Each half has both poles.

questions.q: What is the magnetic force on a charge q moving with velocity v in a field B?
options: q v × B, perpendicular to both v and B
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: Its size is qvB sin θ; a charge at rest or moving along the field feels none.
A is wrong: The magnetic force depends on velocity and is perpendicular to B.
B is wrong: Force is a vector given by a cross product.
D is wrong: That is the electric force.

questions.q: Why can a magnetic force not change a charged particle's speed?
options: Because magnetic fields are always weak
It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
Because it acts only on particles at rest
Because it is always parallel to the velocity
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.4: It only bends the path, giving circular motion in a uniform field.
A is wrong: Even strong magnetic fields do no work on a free charge.
C is wrong: A charge at rest feels no magnetic force.
D is wrong: It is perpendicular, not parallel.

questions.q: What does a current loop in a uniform magnetic field feel?
options: A large net force and no torque
A force pushing it along the field lines
No net force, but a torque turning its dipole moment toward the field
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.7: The torque is the magnetic moment (current times area) crossed with B; this drives a DC motor.
A is wrong: In a uniform field the forces on opposite sides cancel.
B is wrong: The loop does feel a torque.
C is wrong: There is no net force in a uniform field.

questions.q: How do two parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction interact?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.9: Wires with opposite currents repel.
A is wrong: That is for opposite currents.
B is wrong: Each wire is in the other's magnetic field.
D is wrong: The force is attraction along the line between them.

questions.q: A long wire carries 10 A. What is the magnetic field 2 cm away?
options: About 1 × 10⁻⁴ T, about twice the Earth's field
About 50 microteslas, the same as the Earth's field
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 0.02) = 10⁻⁴ T.
A is wrong: That is a thousand times too small.
B is wrong: That is the scale of an MRI magnet.
D is wrong: The result is 100 microteslas, about twice the Earth's field.

questions.q: What is the field inside a long solenoid with n turns per unit length carrying current I?
options: μ₀ n I, nearly uniform along the axis
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.12: Ampère's law applied to a rectangular loop gives this result; the field outside is nearly zero.
A is wrong: That is the field of a straight wire.
B is wrong: The field is nearly zero outside, not inside.
D is wrong: The interior field does not depend on position.

questions.q: What does Faraday's law state?
options: The electromotive force around a loop equals minus the rate of change of magnetic flux through it
A steady magnetic field always produces a current
The magnetic flux through a closed surface is zero
Current produces a magnetic field circling the wire
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: The flux may change through the field, the loop's motion, or its shape.
B is wrong: Only a changing flux induces an electromotive force.
C is wrong: That is Gauss's law for magnetism.
D is wrong: That is Oersted's discovery and Ampère's law.

questions.q: What is Lenz's law?
options: The induced current opposes the change in flux that produced it
The induced current always helps the change in flux
The induced current is always clockwise
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.4: It is the minus sign in Faraday's law, and it expresses energy conservation.
B is wrong: That would create energy from nothing.
C is wrong: Its direction depends on the change in flux.
D is wrong: That is Gauss's law for magnetism.

questions.q: In a transformer, how are the voltages in the two coils related?
options: Their ratio equals the ratio of the numbers of turns
Their ratio is the inverse of the turns ratio
Transformers work with steady direct current
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.7: That is why power is stepped up to high voltage and low current for long-distance transmission.
A is wrong: Transformers exist to change the voltage.
C is wrong: The currents, not the voltages, follow the inverse ratio.
D is wrong: They need a changing flux, so alternating current.

questions.q: A 2 H inductor and a 10 Ω resistor are connected to a battery. What is the time constant of the current's rise?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.9: τ = L/R = 2/10 = 0.2 s.
A is wrong: That multiplies L by R.
B is wrong: That inverts the ratio.
C is wrong: An inductor opposes a sudden change in current.

questions.q: Why did Maxwell add the displacement current to Ampère's law?
options: The law failed for a charging capacitor, where a surface between the plates encloses no current
To explain the resistance of wires
To remove the speed of light from the theory
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.11: The new term, proportional to the rate of change of electric flux, makes a changing electric field produce a magnetic field.
B is wrong: No monopoles are involved.
C is wrong: Resistance is unrelated to this term.
D is wrong: The term led to predicting the speed of light.

questions.q: What speed do Maxwell's equations predict for electromagnetic waves in empty space?
options: 1/√(μ₀ ε₀), about 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of light
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.13: Maxwell recognised that light is an electromagnetic wave.
A is wrong: The speed is the reciprocal of the square root.
C is wrong: Electromagnetic waves are far faster.
D is wrong: The speed is finite and measured.
